content_units: England Rent Increase Check: Your Situation at a Glance
Based on what you described, the increase may   not have followed the usual formal route   for a periodic assured shorthold tenancy in England.
Key points from your facts:
- You are on a   periodic AST  .
- You   did not sign a new agreement  .
- The landlord used an   email  , not the usual formal statutory form.
- Notice was given on   2026-03-01   for an increase starting   2026-04-01  .
For a periodic tenancy in England, a landlord usually increases rent by:
-   Agreement   with the tenant, or
- A formal   Section 13 notice   on the prescribed government form.
An informal email can still be a   proposal  , but it is often   not enough on its own   to impose a unilateral increase if you have not agreed.
Validity Checks for the Increase Notice
Use this checklist to understand whether the process looks proper.
Check   What to look for   Your facts suggest   Why it matters
Tenancy type   Periodic assured shorthold tenancy   Yes   Section 13 usually applies to periodic ASTs
New signed agreement   Any renewal or written variation signed by you   No   Without agreement, landlord usually needs the formal route
Correct form   Official   Form 4 / Section 13 notice     No formal form mentioned   A plain email is often not the prescribed notice
Notice length   Usually at least   1 month   for monthly periodic tenancies   Roughly 1 month   Timing may be close, but form still matters
Start date alignment   Increase date should normally match the tenancy period rules   Needs checking against rent period   Wrong effective date can affect validity
Frequency   Landlord generally cannot use Section 13 more than once in 12 months   Unknown   A repeat increase too soon may be invalid
What to verify closely:
- Whether your tenancy is   monthly periodic   and what day each tenancy period runs from.
- Whether the email clearly said this was a   formal statutory notice   and attached the prescribed form.
- Whether you ever   explicitly accepted   the new rent in writing or by conduct later.
Tenant Response Paths and Practical Next Steps
In practice, tenants usually have a few main options.
Option 1:   Challenge the procedure
- If no valid Section 13 notice was served and you did not agree, you may argue the rent   has not been lawfully increased yet  .
- The old rent may remain payable unless and until a valid process is used.
Option 2:   Negotiate
- You can reply proposing:
- a lower increase,
- a later start date,
- a fixed period before the next review.
- Many rent increases are resolved by agreement rather than formal dispute.
Option 3:   Refer a formal Section 13 increase to tribunal

- If the landlord later serves a valid Section 13 notice, you can usually apply to the   First-tier Tribunal (Property Chamber)   before the new rent start date if you think the amount is above market rent.
- The tribunal does not decide what is “fair” in a general sense; it usually assesses   market rent  .
Option 4:   Accept by agreement
- If you choose to accept, do it clearly in writing and keep the agreed date and amount.
- Be aware that paying the higher rent without protest can sometimes be treated as evidence that you accepted it.
Practical reply approach:
- A short written response can say that you   do not currently agree   to the increase and ask the landlord to confirm the legal basis for it.
- If you are open to compromise, you can also state your   counter-offer  .
Dates and Records to Keep in One Folder
Keep a simple paper trail in case the issue later matters for arrears, deposit deductions, or tribunal timing.
Keep these documents and dates:
-   Current tenancy agreement
- Any renewal paperwork
- The   2026-03-01 email
- Proof of when it was received
- Rent payment records showing the current rent of   £1,250
- Any replies you send about accepting, rejecting, or negotiating
- Evidence of the   tenancy period dates   and normal rent due date
- Any later   formal Section 13 notice   if one is served
Important dates for your timeline:
-   2026-03-01  : landlord email sent
-   2026-04-01  : proposed increase start date
- Your monthly rent due date / tenancy period start date
- Any deadline stated in a later formal notice
- Any tribunal application deadline if a valid Section 13 notice is later served
Useful self-check:
- Note whether you have paid   £1,250 or £1,420   from April onward.
- If you paid the higher amount, note whether you did so   under protest   or without comment.
